questions.q: **MS-DOS**, where you typed commands like DIR and COPY on a black screen, used which type of interface?
questions.solution: DOS used a **command-line interface** — you typed commands; no windows, icons or mouse pointer. Windows brought the GUI style.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT available in the Backstage view opened by the File tab?
questions.solution: Backstage view handles file-level work: New, Open, Save As, Print, Export, Options. **Formatting commands live on the ribbon**, not in Backstage.
questions.shortcut: File tab = file work, not formatting.

questions.q: Output on a **monitor** (seen but not printed) is called a —
questions.solution: **Soft copy** = screen output, temporary and intangible. Paper output is a hard copy.

questions.q: The default orientation of an MS Word page is —
questions.solution: New pages are **Portrait** (taller than wide). Landscape is chosen manually on the Layout tab.

questions.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** Heavy snow began falling on the Srinagar-Leh highway on Tuesday afternoon. **P:** Army teams reached the stranded travellers that evening with blankets and hot food. **Q:** Within hours, hundreds of trucks and cars were stuck near Zojila pass. **R:** Later that day, the vehicles were escorted slowly down to Sonamarg. **S:** By Wednesday morning, snowploughs had cleared a single lane. **6.** The highway was fully reopened only after a week.
questions.solution: Tuesday afternoon (S1) -> within hours **Q** -> that evening **P** -> 'By Wednesday morning' **S**, which sums up the night's clearing -> 'Later that day' **R**, which needs Wednesday. **QPSR**.
questions.shortcut: The by-phrase sums up the night's work; 'Later that day' anchors to Wednesday.

questions.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  MAGNANIMOUS
questions.solution: magn (great) + anim (mind, spirit) → great-spirited = **generous**, ready to forgive. Miserly is the opposite direction.

questions.q: Why does the author mention the farmer in Karnataka?
options: To show that ragi grows well only in Karnataka
To prove that traders always cheat farmers
To illustrate that without mills and assured buying, growing millets does not pay the farmer
To suggest that farmers should stop growing ragi
questions.solution: The sentence before the example says revival is 'not simply a matter of telling people to eat better', and the sentence after says processing units, storage and assured buying must reach villages. The farmer's story (distant mill, low price) illustrates exactly this obstacle. 'Only in Karnataka' and 'always cheat' are extreme and unsupported, and the author wants more millets grown, not less.
questions.shortcut: An example supports the claim next to it. Read one sentence before and after the example.
questions.passage:
For most of the last century, rice and wheat pushed millets off Indian plates. Government buying, cheap ration-shop grain and the prestige attached to 'white' cereals made coarse grains look like food for the poor. Farmers followed the market, and the area under jowar, bajra and ragi shrank steadily.

Millets, however, carry advantages that matter more today than they did fifty years ago. Most varieties need a fraction of the water that paddy demands and can survive on rain alone, which makes them a natural fit for dry districts where groundwater is falling. They are rich in fibre and minerals, and their slow release of sugar suits a population in which diabetes is rising.

Reviving them is not simply a matter of telling people to eat better. A farmer in Karnataka who switched part of her land to ragi found that the nearest mill was forty kilometres away and that traders offered her less than the support price. Unless processing units, storage and assured buying reach the villages, the campaign for millets will remain a slogan in city supermarkets rather than a change in what farmers grow.

questions.q: Parts of a sentence are given as options in order. One part contains an error; the other three are correct. Select the part with the error.
questions.solution: When *every* repeats before both nouns, the subject stays singular: every man and every woman **was counted**. The pair feeling in part 1 tempts the plural, but the rule holds.

questions.q: The Congress split into Moderates and Extremists took place at the **Surat session** of —
questions.solution: The **1907 Surat session** (Rash Behari Ghosh's presidency disputed) split the party; the wings reunited at **Lucknow in 1916**.

questions.q: The **Vernacular Press Act (1878)** — the 'Gagging Act' — was passed by —
questions.solution: **Lytton** gagged Indian-language papers in 1878; **Ripon repealed** it in 1882.

questions.q: Who won India's **first individual Olympic medal**, a wrestling bronze at Helsinki 1952?
questions.solution: **K.D. Jadhav** (wrestling, 1952 Helsinki) - India's first individual Olympic medal. Norman Pritchard had won two athletics silvers for India back in 1900.

questions.q: Which of the following is the only major gold mine still in operation in India?
questions.solution: **Hutti** (Raichur district, Karnataka) is India's only operating large gold mine. **Kolar Gold Fields**, once the deepest mine in India, closed in 2001.

questions.q: The average of five consecutive natural numbers is n. If the next two consecutive numbers are also included, the average of the seven numbers becomes:
questions.solution:
Numbers: $n-2, n-1, n, n+1, n+2$ (sum $5n$). Next two: $n+3, n+4$.
New sum $= 5n + 2n + 7 = 7n + 7$ → average $= n + 1$.
questions.shortcut: Seven consecutive numbers from n−2 to n+4 → middle term is n+1.

questions.q: In a 100 m race A beats B by 5 metres, and in a 100 m race B beats C by 8 metres. By how many metres will A beat C in a 100 m race?
questions.solution:
$\frac{B}{C} = \frac{100}{92}$ → when A runs 100, B runs 95 and C runs $95 \times \frac{92}{100} = 87.4$ m.
Margin $= 100 - 87.4 = 12.6$ m.

questions.q: The complement of an angle of $37^\circ$ is:
questions.solution:
Complement $=90^\circ-37^\circ=53^\circ$.

(Its supplement would be $143^\circ$.)

questions.q: Walking at $\frac{3}{4}$ of his usual speed, a man reaches his office 20 minutes late. His usual time for the journey is:
questions.solution: New time $= \frac{4}{3}t$ ⇒ delay $= \frac{t}{3} = 20$ ⇒ $t = 60$ minutes.

questions.q: Pointing to a girl in a photograph, Rita said, **"She is the daughter of my grandfather's only son."** How is the girl related to Rita?
questions.solution: My grandfather's only son = Rita's father. His daughter = Rita's **sister**. ('Only son' pins the boy as Rita's father, so the girl cannot be a cousin.)
questions.shortcut: Grandfather's only son = your own father — collapse that layer first.

questions.q:
Three of the following four are alike in a certain way and one is different. Find the odd one out.

**BCD, FGH, JKL, OPQ**
questions.solution: All four are three consecutive letters (+1, +1), so steps give no answer. Level two: BCD, FGH, JKL contain **no vowel**; OPQ begins with the vowel **O**. (Also, the first letters B, F, J go +4 each; the next would be N, not O.) → **OPQ**.
questions.shortcut: Same steps everywhere? Check vowels next.

questions.q: Select the related number: **36 : 81 :: 45 : ?**
questions.solution: The digit sum of 36 is 9, and 9² = 81 — **square of the digit sum**. Digit sum of 45 is 9, so 9² = **81**.

questions.q: In a certain code language, **'apples are red' is written 'to na pi'**; **'roses are red' is written 'to na gu'**. What is the code for apples?
questions.solution: 'are' and 'red' are common → codes 'to na'. Sentence 1's leftover word 'apples' takes **pi**.
